Portugal. A small but historically significant nation occupying the western portion of the Iberian Peninsula, bordered by Spain to the east and the Atlantic Ocean to the west and south. Though modest in size and population, Portugal played an outsized role in the Age of Exploration from the 15th to 17th centuries, establishing a vast maritime empire and pioneering transoceanic trade routes to Africa, Asia, and the Americas. Today it is a stable European democracy and European Union member, though its colonial past and economic subordination within Europe continue to shape its identity.

Portugal occupies the westernmost Iberian territory, with a coastline stretching over 1,200 kilometers along the Atlantic. The Tagus River, or Tejo, flows through central Portugal and its estuary defines Lisbon's geography. The kingdom of Portugal emerged in 1139 from Christian reconquest of the peninsula from Muslim rule. It became an independent nation-state in the 12th century, making it one of Europe's oldest nation-states with stable borders.

The Portuguese Age of Exploration from around 1400 to 1600, sponsored by Prince Henry the Navigator and later monarchs, pioneered maritime routes around Africa to India and established trading posts and colonies across four continents. Portuguese navigators, including Vasco da Gama who reached India in 1498 and Ferdinand Magellan who initiated the first circumnavigation from 1519 to 1522, opened global trade routes and established Portugal as a maritime superpower.

The Portuguese Empire at its height controlled territories in Africa including Angola and Mozambique, in Asia including India's Goa, Macau, and East Timor, in South America including Brazil, and elsewhere. It was Europe's longest-lasting colonial empire, persisting until the 1970s. Lisbon, Portugal's capital, is built on hills overlooking the Tagus estuary. It was largely destroyed by an earthquake in 1755 but was rebuilt in a rational grid pattern and remains a historic Atlantic port.

Portugal was ruled by a fascist dictatorship called Estado Novo from 1932 to 1974, during which it brutally resisted decolonization. The Carnation Revolution in 1974 ended dictatorship and eventually led to independence for Angola, Mozambique, and other colonies. Modern Portugal is a stable, affluent member of the European Union and Eurozone, though it has faced economic crises, notably the 2008 financial crisis, and continues to grapple with regional inequality and emigration.
